cim: The Risks of Developing an Artificial Naval Mind | Proceedings - November 2026 Vol. 152/11/1,485
cim_eredeti: The Risks of Developing an Artificial Naval Mind | Proceedings - November 2026 Vol. 152/11/1,485
szoveg_eredeti:
The promise of artificial intelligence is sweeping through the ranks of the U.S. military. In the halls of the Pentagon, posters advise service members and civilians alike to use generative artificial intelligence platforms in nearly everything they do. Developers promise its use will allow the Department of the Navy to gather more information faster. It will provide “decision support” by offering ideas and developing courses of action. In short, it will revolutionize the staff process, policy-making, and strategy for the Navy and Marine Corps.

It all sounds so promising. And it is. Using AI well will grant key advantages in the coming years. However, no military activity comes without risk, and the promise of a faster and easier future is no exception.

Three dangers in particular raise critical questions about how men and women are prepared for the cognitive challenges of leadership in war and peace. First, the use of artificial intelligence may short-circuit millennia-old learning processes central to the development of human cognition. Second, offloading thinking tasks to artificial intelligence may fundamentally change the off-loader’s ability to think critically and make decisions. Third, the entire system of officer formation that begins with basic tasks and builds toward more complex leadership challenges could erode quickly and result in the gradual weakening of professional development. Particularly when it comes to precommissioning officer education and early career growth, these risks suggest a rush to adopt forms of artificial intelligence may weaken the future U.S. Navy and Marine Corps.

Scholars have developed ways of thinking about the differences in how learners engage with a subject. The ICAP framework categorizes student learning as interactive, constructive, active, or passive. Research indicates the strongest learning—in terms of both content recall and conceptual understanding—comes from the interactive and constructive types, in which learners must generate their own ideas and make complex and multilevel connections. For example, a project for which a student is required to do research—finding and reading sources then determining an argument based on them—is both interactive (with the sources) and constructive (developing and communicating an argument).1

Studies examining how students employ artificial intelligence for those tasks show that using AI pushes them almost exclusively into passive learning, the least effective category. If this becomes common, students will retain less domain knowledge. Their ability to identify false, superficial, or biased information will degrade, and they may trust the AI without recognizing or understanding problems with the output. Such passive learning will also reduce students’ abilities to complete constructive tasks on their own. The result: They will have a harder time developing, explaining, and supporting their own ideas.2

Learning correlates with cognitive difficulty. Consider the common metaphor of the brain as a muscle: The emphasis on physical readiness and fitness in the military is something we all understand. But a person does not get stronger by going to the gym to watch other people lift weights. And a person is unlikely to increase cardiovascular fitness by using the electric motor on an ebike instead of actually pedaling. Human brains, like muscles, prefer to do things the easy way. But to learn something or improve cognitive ability requires you to do difficult or complex things. Like an ebike, artificial intelligence is designed to make life easier, in this case through a process called cognitive offloading. It may, however, have a dramatically negative effect on a future leader’s ability to analyze a situation and make decisions without AI’s support.

Critical thinking is one of those phrases that rings out across discussions of education and artificial intelligence. Some hear “critical” and think “important.” But critical thinking is about the word’s other usages: criticizing, analyzing, evaluating, and synthesizing information. Logically, if AI reduces a learner’s engagement to a passive level, and cognitive offloading increases, it will reduce the learner’s ability or inclination to do his or her own thinking.

Recent studies have begun to examine this logic. The results have been strongly negative. In one study, MIT researchers assigned student volunteers to three groups. One completed the test project—write an essay—using a large language model (LLM) in all elements of their work. Another was permitted to use only traditional internet search engines. And a third was “brain only.”

After the essays were submitted, the volunteers were tested on a series of cognitive tasks. The results were stark. Minutes after submitting their essays, only 16 percent of LLM users could quote something from their work, but 88 percent of the brain-only group could do so. The researchers wrote that the LLM group performed worse than the other groups at all levels. Through multiple iterations, the AI-using group had degraded neural connectivity even when asked to complete additional tasks unassisted by AI. In short, the brain did not return to baseline—it stayed degraded.3 Using LLMs might be making students less capable of intelligent tasks.

A second study examined the critical thinking ability of almost 700 participants and discovered significant degradation among regular users of AI tools. It suggested trust in AI grew with higher levels of use, independent of whether the AI was giving correct answers. In addition, it suggested that users age 25 and younger trusted the AI at much higher levels and saw significant reductions in measured thinking scores after AI use.4

These are initial studies with limited sample sizes; the findings are preliminary. They also are disturbing. If producing officers with the “potential for future development in mind and character to assume the highest responsibilities of command, citizenship and government” is the mission of the Naval Academy, NROTC, and the other commissioning sources, then indiscriminate use of artificial intelligence could create foundational challenges.5

Recent examinations of early development suggest AI use threatens to disrupt its apprenticeship elements. It may result in the loss of tacit knowledge and reduce the accumulation of contextual wisdom. All these problems threaten the establishment of a modern workforce and the formation of the next generation of naval leaders.

Joining a profession brings with it an apprenticeship requirement. This is true of many white-collar industries, such as financial services and IT. Drafting basic documents, summarizing incoming data, analyzing sources or spreadsheets; all are typical grunt work for entry-level team members. Naval officers face similar tasks—writing messages, drafting fitness reports and enlisted evals, and completing record-keeping.6

While these tasks might superficially appear to fulfill purely generative needs, they also build foundational knowledge and contextual understanding. Junior officers who use AI to scrape the brag sheets of their sailors to create performance evaluations at the touch of a button will complete the process more quickly. However, they also will spend less time thinking about their sailors or Marines. Yes, an eval requires a lot of tiresome effort—reviewing details and ensuring the data is in the right fields—but it results in better knowledge of the women and men in the officers’ divisions and platoons. In addition, having a generative AI write the bullets is also likely to produce homogenized results, where all evals start to look even more alike than they do already. The point of a generative AI is to come up with the average answer, and you likely want your sailor to look above average when he or she is going up for chief petty officer selection.

Using generative AI risks making junior-level work less human-centric and more machine-mediated.
